127382.q: What does the verdict “major revision” mean in peer review?
a: Substantial revision needed, then a new review
The article is accepted straight away
127382.e: With a “major revision”, the authors must rework important points, for example by adding analyses. After that, the article is usually reviewed again.
127382.m: A major revision is not yet an acceptance.

127383.q: Which weakness is peer review often accused of?
a: It does not reliably detect fraud
It is carried out by laypeople
127383.e: Reviewers usually only see the article and not the raw data. Deliberate fraud or errors can therefore go undetected.
127383.m: Peer review is a quality check, but no protection against every fraud.

a: Reviews and sometimes names are made public
127384.e: In open peer review, the names of the reviewers or the reviews themselves are published. This is meant to encourage transparency and care.
127384.m: Open peer review makes the review process transparent.

127385.q: What does the Swiss National Science Foundation use peer review for?
127385.e: The SNSF has applications for research funding assessed by external experts. On this basis, it decides on funding.
127385.m: Research funding applications are also assessed by peer review.

127386.q: Which society published one of the first scientific journals, the Philosophical Transactions, in 1665?
127386.e: The Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society in London have appeared since 1665. They are regarded as the oldest scientific journal still in existence.
127386.m: The Royal Society has published one of the oldest scientific journals since 1665.

127387.q: What do preprints on servers such as bioRxiv receive so that they can be cited permanently?
127387.e: A DOI (Digital Object Identifier) is a permanent identifier for digital documents. It means even a preprint can be clearly cited and found again.
127387.m: A DOI makes scientific documents permanently findable.

127388.q: What is the name of the preprint server founded in 1991 that is used mainly in physics and mathematics?
127388.e: arXiv was founded in 1991 by Paul Ginsparg. Physics, mathematics and computer science have used it heavily for decades.
127388.m: arXiv is the most important preprint server for physics and mathematics.

127389.q: Which preprint server specialises in medicine and health sciences?
127389.e: medRxiv accepts preprints from medicine and the health sciences. It became especially well known during the Covid-19 pandemic.
127389.m: medRxiv is a preprint server for medicine.

127390.q: Which preprint server specialises in biology?
127390.e: bioRxiv was founded by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory and accepts work from all areas of biology.
127390.m: bioRxiv is a preprint server for biology.

127391.q: What is the most important advantage of preprints?
127391.e: Peer review can take months. Preprints make results available immediately, which can be important, for example, in a pandemic.
127391.m: Preprints make research available more quickly.

127392.q: What should the media pay particular attention to when reporting on preprints?
a: Pointing out that they have not been peer reviewed
Presenting them as the final truth
127392.e: Preprints have not yet been through peer review and may contain errors. Serious reports make this clear and get independent opinions.
127392.m: Reports on preprints should mention that they have not been reviewed.

127393.q: What happened to the number of preprints at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic?
127393.e: In 2020, a great many studies on Covid-19 were first published as preprints. This sped up the exchange of ideas, but also spread flawed results.
127393.m: During the pandemic, the number of preprints rose sharply.

127394.q: What usually happens to a preprint when the work later appears in a journal?
a: It is linked to the published version
127394.e: Many preprint servers link to the later journal version. This way readers find the peer-reviewed version.
127394.m: Preprints are often linked to the later journal version.

127395.q: What is the aim of open science?
a: Making research openly and transparently accessible
127395.e: Open science aims to make publications, data, methods and software as freely accessible as possible. This makes checking and reuse easier.
127395.m: Open science makes research open and checkable.

127396.e: Open access means that scientific publications can be read free of charge on the internet by everyone. Readers do not need a subscription.
127396.m: Open access makes scientific articles free to read.

127397.q: What is the “green route” to open access?
127397.e: On the green route, researchers also put a version of their article in a freely accessible repository. On the gold route, the article appears openly in the journal itself.
127397.m: The green route to open access is self-archiving.

127398.q: Which research organisation near Geneva helps run the open repository Zenodo?
127398.e: Zenodo was built by CERN together with the European project OpenAIRE. Researchers can store data, software and publications there free of charge.
127398.m: Zenodo is an open repository that CERN helps to run.

127399.q: What does the F in the FAIR principles for research data stand for?
127399.e: FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. Data should be findable, accessible, linkable and reusable.
127399.m: According to the FAIR principles, research data should be findable and reusable.

127400.q: What does the Swiss National Science Foundation require of publications from projects it funds?
a: They may only appear in print
127400.e: The SNSF requires the researchers it funds to publish their results in open access in principle. Under certain conditions it covers the costs.
127400.m: The SNSF requires open access for the publications it funds.

127401.q: What does open data mean in research?
a: Making raw data freely available for reuse
127401.e: With open data, research data is made available publicly and with clear rights of use. Others can then check and reuse results.
127401.m: Open data means making research data freely available.

a: Journals that collect fees without real peer review
Publishers that only print books about animals
127402.e: Predatory journals pose as reputable open-access journals, charge fees and skip serious quality checks. Articles there are often not very trustworthy.
127402.m: Predatory journals collect fees without seriously checking articles.

127403.q: What is the main task of science journalism?
a: Explaining research clearly and putting it in critical context
127403.e: Science journalists explain research for a wide audience. They also check critically how robust results are.
127403.m: Science journalism explains research and puts it in critical context.

127404.q: What is meant by “false balance” in science journalism?
a: Giving a minority view the same weight as the consensus
Presenting two studies in a balanced way
127404.e: With false balance, fringe positions are given the same weight as a broad research consensus, for example on climate change. This gives a false picture of the facts.
127404.m: False balance wrongly presents fringe opinions as equal to the consensus.

127405.q: What is an embargo at scientific journals?
a: The media may only report from a certain time
127405.e: Journals give journalists articles in advance so that they can do their research. But they may only report once the embargo has expired.
127405.m: An embargo sets when the media may report on a study.

127406.q: Which common mistake arises when a cause is directly concluded from a statistical connection?
a: Confusing the mean and the median
127406.e: The fact that two things occur together does not prove that one causes the other. Often there is a third factor behind it.
127406.m: A correlation is not yet proof of a cause.

127407.q: Which organisation quickly provides the media with expert opinions on current research topics?
127407.e: There are Science Media Centres in the United Kingdom and Germany, for example. They collect statements from independent researchers for newsrooms.
127407.m: Science Media Centres help the media with voices from research.

127408.q: Why should journalists not just read a university's press release?
127408.e: Studies showed that exaggerations in media reports are often already found in press releases. Looking at the original study helps to check the claims.
127408.m: For good science journalism, it is worth looking at the original study.

127409.q: What should a good report about a study on mice make clear?
a: That the results cannot be transferred directly to humans
That the study automatically applies to humans
That mice are not laboratory animals
That animal studies are never useful
127409.e: Many results from animal studies are not confirmed in humans. Serious reports name the study model and carefully put its importance in context.
127409.m: Animal studies cannot be transferred directly to humans.

127410.q: What is the name of SRF's science programme on television?
127410.e: “Einstein” is the science programme of Swiss television SRF. Galileo, Quarks and Terra X are programmes on German channels.

127411.q: What is meant by citizen science?
127411.e: In citizen science, interested laypeople collect or analyse data for research projects. This produces large data sets.
127411.m: In citizen science, laypeople help with research.

127412.q: What did volunteers do in the Galaxy Zoo project?
127412.e: In Galaxy Zoo, volunteers classified images of galaxies online, for example as spiral or elliptical. New objects were discovered along the way too.
127412.m: In Galaxy Zoo, laypeople sorted galaxies by their shape.

a: An online game about protein folding
127413.e: In Foldit, players solve puzzles by folding protein structures. Their solutions helped researchers to work out structures.
127413.m: In the game Foldit, players help to find protein structures.

127414.q: Which online platform brings together many citizen science projects such as Galaxy Zoo?
127414.e: Zooniverse grew out of Galaxy Zoo and today offers many projects, from astronomy to history. Volunteers can take part online there.
127414.m: Zooniverse is a large platform for citizen science.

127415.q: Which Swiss organisation runs the join-in campaign “Hour of the Garden Birds”?
127415.e: In the “Hour of the Garden Birds”, volunteers count the birds in their garden or park for one hour and report them. The data shows trends in common species.
127415.m: In the “Hour of the Garden Birds”, volunteers count birds for research.

127416.q: Which facility for citizen science do the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich run together?
127416.e: The Citizen Science Center Zurich supports projects in which members of the public take part in research. It is a joint facility of UZH and ETH Zurich.
127416.m: UZH and ETH jointly run the Citizen Science Center Zurich.

127417.q: What did participants contribute to SETI@home?
127417.e: SETI@home used unused computing time on private computers to search radio signals for signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. This is called distributed computing.
127417.m: In SETI@home, volunteers provided computing power.

127418.q: Which Swiss institution relies heavily on volunteer observers for its breeding bird atlases?
a: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach
127418.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach works with thousands of volunteers. Their observations form the basis for atlases and population trends.
127418.m: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach works closely with volunteer observers.

127419.q: Which risk must be watched especially carefully with citizen science data?
127419.e: Laypeople have different levels of experience, and observations are not always collected in the same way. Projects therefore use training, multiple ratings and statistics.
127419.m: In citizen science, data quality must be carefully ensured.

a: Short talks about research that the audience rates
127420.e: At a science slam, researchers present their work in a short time in an entertaining and understandable way. The audience chooses the best contribution.
127420.m: At a science slam, researchers explain their work briefly and entertainingly.

127421.q: Which event format was the model for the science slam?
127421.e: As at a poetry slam, several speakers perform one after another and the audience decides. Instead of poems, it is about research.
127421.m: The science slam is modelled on the poetry slam.

127422.q: What is typically the maximum length of a contribution at a science slam?
127422.e: A science slam performance usually has around ten minutes available. The short time forces you to concentrate on what really matters.
127422.m: A science slam contribution usually lasts around ten minutes.

127423.q: Who usually rates the contributions at a science slam?
127423.e: The audience usually decides the winner, for example with applause or voting cards. Clarity, content and entertainment are rated.
127423.m: At a science slam, the audience decides.

127424.q: What is the name of the competition in which doctoral students present their research project with just one slide in a very short time?
127424.e: In Three Minute Thesis, doctoral students have three minutes and one slide. In Pecha Kucha, by contrast, you show 20 images for 20 seconds each.
127424.m: In Three Minute Thesis, you explain a doctorate in three minutes.

127425.q: What is the main aim of a science slam?
a: Bringing research closer to a wide audience
127425.e: Science slams aim to lower barriers and show that research can be exciting. At the same time, researchers practise explaining things clearly.
127425.m: Science slams make research accessible to everyone.

127426.q: Which international science communication competition with short performances is supported by the British Council?
127426.e: At FameLab, young researchers explain a topic in a few minutes without slides. The competition is held in many countries.
127426.m: FameLab is an international competition for short science talks.

127427.q: Which universities jointly organise the Scientifica in Zurich?
a: University of Zurich and ETH Zurich
University of Basel and ETH Zurich
127427.e: The Scientifica, the Zurich science days, is organised jointly by the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich. It is aimed at the general public.
127427.m: The Scientifica is a joint event of UZH and ETH Zurich.

a: A science festival for the public
A trade fair only for companies
127428.e: At the Scientifica, researchers show their work with exhibitions, experiments, short talks and conversations. It aims to encourage dialogue with the public.
127428.m: At the Scientifica, researchers present their work to the public.

127429.q: How much does it cost the public to visit the Scientifica?
127429.e: The Zurich science days are free to attend. This is meant to reach as many people as possible, including families.
127429.m: Entry to the Scientifica is free.

127430.q: Where do the Scientifica events mainly take place?
a: In the main buildings of UZH and ETH in the city centre
127430.e: The Scientifica uses the buildings of the university and ETH in Zurich's university quarter. There are stands, talks and hands-on activities there.
127430.m: The Scientifica takes place in Zurich's university quarter.

127431.q: What is typical of every edition of the Scientifica?
127431.e: Each edition of the Scientifica places the contributions under an overall theme. Researchers from different subjects show their view of it.
127431.m: Each Scientifica has its own main theme.

127432.q: Which Swiss foundation works nationwide for dialogue between science and society?
127432.e: Since the late 1990s, the Science et Cité foundation has promoted exchange between research and the public. It also supports citizen science projects.
127432.m: Science et Cité promotes dialogue between science and society.

127433.q: Which target group does the Scientifica explicitly address besides adults?
127433.e: The Scientifica offers its own activities for children, young people and school classes, such as hands-on experiments. The whole family should experience research.
127433.m: The Scientifica also has activities for children and young people.

127434.q: In which city was the journal Nature founded?
127434.e: Nature first appeared in 1869 in London. It is still one of the most respected scientific journals today.
127434.m: The journal Nature was founded in London.

127435.q: In which year did the first issue of Nature appear?
127435.e: The first issue of Nature appeared in November 1869. This makes it one of the oldest scientific weeklies still in existence.

127436.q: What does it mean that research articles in Nature go through peer review?
a: Other experts check them before publication
They are only corrected by the editors
They are first printed in a newspaper
127436.e: In peer review, independent researchers from the same field assess an article. Only if it passes their checks is it published.
127436.m: In peer review, experts check an article before publication.

127437.q: Which famous article on the structure of DNA appeared in Nature in 1953?
a: The article by Watson and Crick
The article by Darwin and Wallace
The article by Bohr and Heisenberg
The article by Curie and Becquerel
127437.e: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix of DNA in Nature. The short article is regarded as one of the most important in biology.
127437.m: Watson and Crick published the DNA double helix in Nature in 1953.

127438.e: Nature appears every week with research articles, news and comment. Many articles are also available online in advance.

127439.e: Nature belongs to the publishing group Springer Nature. It also publishes many other scientific journals.
127439.m: Nature is published today by Springer Nature.

127440.q: What is the name of Nature's multidisciplinary open-access sister journal?
127440.e: Nature Communications publishes freely accessible research from all the natural and life sciences. It belongs to the same publishing family as Nature.
127440.m: Nature Communications is an open-access journal in the Nature family.

127441.q: Which organisation publishes the journal Science?
127441.e: Science is published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). This is one of the largest scientific organisations in the world.
127441.m: Science is published by the AAAS.

127442.q: In which century was the journal Science founded?
127442.e: Science was founded in 1880 in New York and later became the journal of the AAAS. Along with Nature, it is one of the best-known scientific journals.
127442.m: Science has appeared since the 19th century.

127443.q: Which famous inventor gave financial support to the founding of Science?
127443.e: In the early days, Thomas Edison gave the founder John Michels money for the journal. Later, Alexander Graham Bell also supported it.

127444.q: What is the name of the yearly award with which Science names the most important discovery of the year?
127444.e: At the end of the year, the editors of Science choose a “Breakthrough of the Year” and other important advances. The choice attracts attention worldwide.
127444.m: Science names a breakthrough of the year every year.

127445.q: In which city does the AAAS, the publisher of Science, have its headquarters?
127445.e: The AAAS is based in Washington, D.C. The journal Science is also run from there.
127445.m: The AAAS is based in Washington, D.C.

127446.q: What is the name of the freely accessible sister journal of Science?
127446.e: Science Advances is an open-access journal of the AAAS. It publishes research from all fields.
127446.m: Science Advances is the open-access sister of Science.

127447.q: What kind of content does Science also publish besides research articles?
127447.e: As well as peer-reviewed research articles, Science contains a news section, comment pieces and review articles. This means it also speaks to a wider expert audience.
127447.m: Science contains research articles, news and comment.

127448.q: What does the journal impact factor of a journal like Science measure?
a: How often its articles are cited on average
The number of pages per issue
127448.e: The impact factor shows how often a journal's articles from the two previous years are cited on average. It says little about the quality of an individual article.
127448.m: The impact factor measures how often a journal's articles are cited.

127449.e: Altmetrics count, for example, mentions in social media, news, blogs, Wikipedia or reference managers. They complement traditional citation counts.
127449.m: Altmetrics measure how much attention research gets online.

127450.q: What does the part “alt” in altmetrics stand for?
127450.e: Altmetrics are alternative metrics to the traditional citation figures. The term became known around 2010 through a manifesto.
127450.m: Altmetrics are alternative measures of the impact of research.

127451.q: Which advantage is attributed to altmetrics compared with citations?
a: They show the response very quickly
127451.e: Citations build up over years, while online mentions can be measured after just days. Altmetrics also show impact outside the expert world.
127451.m: Altmetrics show the response to research earlier than citations.

127452.q: Which important criticism is made of altmetrics?
a: They only take libraries into account
127452.e: Controversial or flawed studies can also get a lot of online attention. In addition, mentions can be inflated artificially, for example by bots.
127452.m: A lot of attention does not automatically mean good research.

127453.q: What does a researcher's h-index measure?
a: The number h of papers with at least h citations
The number of social media followers
The size of her research budget
The number of her doctoral students
127453.e: An h-index of 20 means that 20 papers have each been cited at least 20 times. The physicist Jorge Hirsch proposed it in 2005.
127453.m: The h-index combines the number of publications with how often they are cited.

127454.q: What does the journal impact factor measure?
a: How often a journal's articles are cited on average
How many copies of a journal are sold
How many researchers work at a journal
How often a journal is mentioned online
127454.e: The impact factor divides the citations in one year by the number of articles from the two previous years. It was developed by Eugene Garfield.
127454.m: The impact factor measures how often a journal is cited.

127455.q: Which source is typically recorded by altmetrics?
127455.e: Altmetrics services analyse, for example, news portals, blogs, policy documents and social networks. An attention score is produced from this.
127455.m: Altmetrics analyse news and social media, among other things.

127456.q: What does the coloured “doughnut” from the provider Altmetric show for an article?
a: Which sources the attention comes from
127456.e: The colours of the doughnut stand for different sources such as news, blogs or social media. In the middle is a combined attention score.
127456.m: The Altmetric doughnut shows the sources of online attention.

127457.q: What does the term infodemic mean?
a: An overload of information, much of it false
A gap in knowledge at schools
127457.e: In an infodemic, a huge amount of information spreads, including false or misleading information, faster than it can be checked. This makes sensible decisions harder.
127457.m: An infodemic is a flood of information, some of it false.

127458.q: Which organisation made the term infodemic well known in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic?
127458.e: At the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, the WHO explicitly warned of an infodemic. It set up its own programmes against false information.
127458.m: In 2020, the WHO warned of an infodemic.

a: Warning people in advance about manipulation techniques
Blocking whole countries on the internet
127459.e: In prebunking, people learn about the typical tricks of false information before they come across them. Like a vaccination, this is meant to make them more resistant.
127459.m: Prebunking makes people resistant to false information in advance.

a: Disproving a piece of false information afterwards
127460.e: In debunking, a false claim that has already spread is disproved with facts. It works especially well when the correct information is clearly in the foreground.
127460.m: Debunking disproves false information after the event.

127461.q: What do you call a space on social media in which you hear almost only opinions that match your own?
127461.e: In an echo chamber, like-minded people confirm each other's views, and facts that differ hardly get through. This encourages the spread of false information.
127461.m: In an echo chamber, you mostly hear your own opinion confirmed.

127462.q: Which skill helps individuals most to find their way in an infodemic?
a: Sharing as many posts as possible
127462.e: Anyone who checks who is behind a piece of information and whether reliable sources confirm it is less likely to fall for false reports. This is called information or media literacy.
127462.m: Checking sources critically protects against false information.

127463.q: What is the difference between healthy scepticism and science denial?
a: Scepticism checks evidence, denial ignores it
127463.e: Healthy scepticism asks for evidence and is ready to change its mind when the data is good. Denial sticks to a position, even against clear evidence.
127463.m: Healthy scepticism can be convinced by evidence.

127464.q: Which regularly conducted survey examines the Swiss population's relationship with science?
127464.e: Since 2016, the Science Barometer Switzerland has asked the population every few years about their trust in and interest in science. It shows that a majority tends to trust science.
127464.m: The Science Barometer measures how much Switzerland trusts science.

127465.q: What does “cherry picking” mean in debates about science?
a: Choosing only the data that fits
127465.e: In cherry picking, only the studies or data that support your own opinion are mentioned. Contradictory findings are kept quiet.
127465.m: Cherry picking shows only the data that fits your own opinion.

127466.q: Which strategy does the book Merchants of Doubt describe?
127466.e: Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway show how some players deliberately spread doubt about research on tobacco or climate change. The aim was to delay regulation.
127466.m: Deliberately sown doubt can undermine scientific findings.

127467.q: Which of Robert Merton's norms of science describes that all claims are critically examined?
127467.e: Merton named four norms of science. Organised scepticism requires every claim to be checked by the community before it is accepted.
127467.m: Organised scepticism is one of the basic norms of science.

127468.q: Which technique of science denial uses supposed experts without real expertise?
127468.e: Denial campaigns often quote people with titles from other fields, or small groups, as a counter-voice to the consensus. This creates the impression of an open debate.
127468.m: Fake experts are meant to make a research consensus look questionable.

127469.q: What is an “impossible expectation” as a strategy of denial?
127469.e: Anyone who demands one hundred per cent certainty can reject any finding, because science always delivers probabilities. This is often used with climate change.
127469.m: Science delivers well-supported statements, but not absolute certainty.

127470.q: Which communication strategy is seen as fairly helpful when dealing with people who are sceptical of science?
a: Listening and engaging with their values
127470.e: Studies show that mockery and lecturing can strengthen resistance. Listening respectfully and connecting with shared values increase the chance of a real exchange.
127470.m: Listening respectfully helps in conversations with sceptical people.

127471.q: Which fields does the journal Nature cover?
a: All the natural and life sciences
127471.e: Nature is a multidisciplinary journal and publishes research from physics and biology to the earth sciences. There are also specialised sister journals.
127471.m: Nature is a multidisciplinary scientific journal.

127472.q: In which country did the first science slams take place?
127472.e: The first science slams were held in Germany. From there, the format spread to many other countries, including Switzerland.
127472.m: The science slam comes from Germany.

127473.q: Which discussion format, in which researchers talk with the audience in a relaxed setting, is often part of science festivals such as the Scientifica?
127473.e: In a science café, researchers and the audience sit together and discuss things as equals. The format originally comes from the United Kingdom and France.
127473.m: In a science café, researchers talk informally with the audience.

127474.q: What is the effect called when algorithms mainly show users content that matches their previous preferences?
127474.e: The term filter bubble was coined by Eli Pariser. Personalised algorithms can mean that contradicting information becomes visible less often.
127474.m: A filter bubble is created by personalised algorithms.

127475.q: Which technique of denial declares a broad research consensus to be a secret plot?
127475.e: Anyone who presents a consensus as a conspiracy can dismiss any counter-evidence as part of the plot. This makes such stories almost impossible to disprove.
127475.m: Conspiracy theories make themselves immune to counter-evidence.

127476.q: What is the maximum time a patent can be kept in force in Switzerland and Europe (without special extensions)?
127476.e: The maximum term of protection for a patent is 20 years from the filing date. After that, the invention becomes free and anyone may use it.
127476.m: A patent protects an invention for at most 20 years.

127477.q: Which three requirements must an invention basically meet to be patentable?
127477.e: An invention must be new, must not be obvious to an expert from the state of the art and must be industrially applicable.
127477.m: Only what is new, inventive and industrially applicable can be patented.

127478.q: What does the inventor give society in return for patent protection?
a: He pays part of the profit to the state
He must give the invention away for free
127478.e: The patent specification is published so that others can learn from the invention and build on it once the protection ends. In return, the owner gets an exclusive right for a limited time.
127478.m: A patent is a trade of disclosure for time-limited protection.

127479.q: What right does a patent mainly give its owner?
a: To forbid others from using it commercially
To have the invention funded by the state
To register a trade mark for free
127479.e: A patent is a right to forbid: the owner can stop third parties from commercially making, selling or using the invention. They can also grant this right to others by licence.
127479.m: A patent lets you forbid others from using an invention.

127480.q: What usually happens to a patent application, even if the patent has not yet been granted?
a: It is published after a fixed period
It is deleted after a year
It is sold to competing firms
127480.e: Patent applications are usually published 18 months after the first filing date. This way the public learns about new inventions early.
127480.m: Patent applications become public after a set period.

127481.q: Two people make the same invention independently of each other. Who gets the patent in Europe?
127481.e: In Europe, the first-to-file principle applies: what matters is the filing date, not the date of the invention. That is why companies file inventions as early as possible.
127481.m: With patents, what counts is who files first.

127482.q: What does the principle of territoriality mean in patent law?
a: A patent only has effect in the states for which it was granted
Patents only apply within one canton
Only plots of land can be patented
A patent only applies where the inventor lives
127482.e: A patent is a national protective right. Anyone who wants protection in several countries needs a patent in each of them, for example via the European Patent Office in Munich.
127482.m: A patent only protects in the countries where it applies.

127483.q: What can basically NOT be patented under European patent law?
127483.e: Under the European Patent Convention, discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods are not regarded as inventions. Technical teachings such as devices or processes can be patented.
127483.m: Theories and discoveries are not patentable inventions.

127484.q: In which city is the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property (IPI) based?
127484.e: The IPI is based in Bern. It is the central Swiss authority for patents, trade marks and designs.
127484.m: The Swiss office for intellectual property is in Bern.

127485.q: What legal form does the IPI have?
a: An independent federal institution under public law
A company owned by the cantons
127485.e: The IPI is a federal institution under public law with its own legal personality. It is funded largely by fees and not by taxes.
127485.m: The IPI is an independent federal institution.

127486.q: Which protective right arises automatically in Switzerland and is NOT registered with the IPI?
127486.e: Copyright in a work arises when it is created, without registration. Patents, trade marks and designs, on the other hand, must be filed and registered with the IPI.
127486.m: Copyright does not need to be registered.

127487.q: How long does a trade mark registered with the IPI last before it must be renewed?
127487.e: A Swiss trade mark is protected for 10 years from filing. After that, it can be renewed as often as you like, for 10 years each time.
127487.m: A trade mark can be renewed every ten years without limit.

127488.q: What does a design registered with the IPI protect?
a: The outward appearance of a product
The technical function of an invention
The name of a company or product
127488.e: A design protects the look, such as the shape, colour or pattern of a product. Technical inventions are protected by patents, names and logos by trade marks, texts by copyright. A design is protected for at most 25 years.
127488.m: A design protects how a product looks.

127489.q: What is the name of the IPI's public online database for Swiss protective rights?
127489.e: In Swissreg you can look up registered Swiss patents, trade marks and designs. Zefix, on the other hand, is the central business name index of the commercial register.
127489.m: Protective rights can be found in the Swissreg database.

127490.q: Under the Swissness rules, at least what share of the manufacturing costs of industrial products must be incurred in Switzerland?
127490.e: Since the Swissness legislation, at least 60 per cent of the manufacturing costs of industrial products must be incurred in Switzerland. The IPI provides information on these rules about indications of origin.
127490.m: For “Swiss made” on industrial products, 60 per cent of the manufacturing costs must be Swiss.

127491.q: Besides granting protective rights, what else is the IPI responsible for?
127491.e: The IPI drafts bills on patent, trade mark, design and copyright law and represents Switzerland in international bodies on intellectual property. Research funding is awarded by other bodies.
127491.m: The IPI also helps shape Swiss laws on intellectual property.

127492.q: In which year did Albert Einstein start his job at the Federal Office for Intellectual Property in Bern?
127492.e: In 1902, Einstein started as a technical expert, third class, at the Bern patent office. There he examined patent applications, mainly for electrical devices.
127492.m: Einstein joined the patent office in Bern in 1902.

127493.q: What work did Albert Einstein do at the Bern patent office?
a: He ran the university's physics department
He built clocks for the Federal Railways
127493.e: As a technical expert, Einstein assessed patent applications, mainly for electrical devices. On the side, he worked on his own theories.

127494.q: What is the year 1905 called, in which Einstein published several groundbreaking papers alongside his work at the patent office?
127494.e: In 1905, Einstein published papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and the special theory of relativity, among others. It is known as the “miracle year”.

127495.q: What did Einstein receive the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for?
a: For the general theory of relativity
127495.e: The Nobel Committee explicitly honoured his explanation of the photoelectric effect, not the theory of relativity. The prize for 1921 was only awarded in 1922.
127495.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect.

127496.q: Why did Einstein leave the patent office in Bern in 1909?
a: He became a professor at the University of Zurich
He became a diplomat in Berlin
127496.e: In 1909, Einstein became associate professor of theoretical physics at the University of Zurich. This was the start of his academic career.
127496.m: In 1909, Einstein moved from the patent office to the University of Zurich.

127497.q: Where had Albert Einstein studied before he came to the Bern patent office?
a: At the Polytechnic in Zurich, today's ETH
127497.e: In 1900, Einstein completed his studies as a teacher of mathematics and physics at the Federal Polytechnic. There he also met Marcel Grossmann.
127497.m: Einstein studied at what is now ETH Zurich.

127498.q: Which device did Einstein patent together with Leo Szilard?
127498.e: The Einstein-Szilard refrigerator worked without a compressor with moving parts. It was patented but hardly ever mass-produced.
127498.m: Einstein was not only an examiner but also a patent holder himself.

127499.q: Where in Bern can you visit the flat today where Einstein lived during his time at the patent office?
a: In the Einstein House on Kramgasse
127499.e: Einstein lived at Kramgasse 49 in Bern's old town from 1903 to 1905. Today the flat is a museum, the Einstein House.
127499.m: The Einstein House is on Kramgasse in Bern.

127500.q: What is meant by a university spin-off such as an ETH spin-off?
a: A company that uses the university's research results commercially
A branch of a foreign university
127500.e: A spin-off is founded by researchers to bring knowledge or technologies from the university to market. It often uses the university's patents under licence.
127500.m: A spin-off brings research from the university to market.

127501.q: What does the ETH spin-off Climeworks develop?
a: Plants that filter CO2 directly from the air
127501.e: Climeworks builds so-called direct air capture plants that remove carbon dioxide from the surrounding air. Larger plants are in Iceland, where the CO2 is stored in rock.
127501.m: Climeworks takes CO2 out of the air.

127502.q: In which country does Climeworks run its well-known large plants for storing CO2 underground?
127502.e: The Orca and Mammoth plants are in Iceland. The captured CO2 is pumped into basalt rock there, where it mineralises.
127502.m: Climeworks stores CO2 in Iceland's basalt.

127503.q: What is the ETH spin-off Sensirion known for internationally?
a: Sensors, for example for humidity and gases
127503.e: Sensirion was founded in Stäfa in the late 1990s and makes sensors for humidity, temperature, gases and flow. These are found, for example, in cars and appliances.
127503.m: Sensirion is an ETH spin-off for sensors.

127504.q: What is the name of the ETH Zurich programme that gives financial support to researchers with a business idea before they found a company?
127504.e: With the Pioneer Fellowships, researchers receive money and coaching to develop a technology further until they found a spin-off.
127504.m: Pioneer Fellowships help to found ETH spin-offs.

127505.q: How does a spin-off typically get the right to use a university patent?
a: Through a licence agreement with the university
By simply copying the patent specification
By applying to the Federal Supreme Court
127505.e: The university usually owns the patents from its research. The spin-off receives the right to use them by licence and pays fees for it or gives up shares in the company.
127505.m: Spin-offs use university patents through licences.

127506.q: Which ETH Zurich spin-off offers software for scanning barcodes with a smartphone?
127506.e: Scandit develops software that lets smartphone cameras capture barcodes quickly, for example in retail and logistics.
127506.m: Scandit turns the smartphone into a barcode scanner.

127507.q: Which four research institutes belong to the ETH Domain?
a: University of Bern and University of Basel
Innosuisse and the National Science Foundation
127507.e: Besides the two universities, the ETH Domain includes the four research institutes Paul Scherrer Institute, WSL, Empa and Eawag. These also produce spin-offs.
127507.m: The ETH Domain includes four research institutes: PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag.

a: Transferring research knowledge into commercial use
Moving a lab into a new building
127508.e: In technology transfer, findings from universities and research institutes reach companies, for example through licences, partnerships or spin-offs.
127508.m: Technology transfer brings research into practice.

127509.q: What is the name of the ETH Zurich office that patents inventions, grants licences and supports spin-offs?
127509.e: ETH transfer is the technology transfer office of ETH Zurich. It acts as a go-between for researchers and companies and concludes licence and research agreements.
127509.m: At ETH, ETH transfer looks after technology transfer.

a: A network of innovation parks at several locations in Switzerland
A yearly inventors' competition on television
127510.e: Several regional innovation parks work under the umbrella of Switzerland Innovation. There, universities and companies are meant to research new technologies together.
127510.m: Switzerland Innovation links innovation parks across Switzerland.

127511.q: What is the task of Innosuisse?
a: It promotes innovation, for example projects between universities and firms
127511.e: Innosuisse is the Swiss Innovation Agency. It supports projects in which research and business work together, and it helps start-ups.

127512.q: What is the scale from 1 to 9 called that describes how far a technology has developed, from the basic principle to a proven system?
127512.e: Technology Readiness Levels were introduced by NASA. Level 1 means basic principles observed, level 9 a system proven in operation.
127512.m: The TRL value shows how mature a technology is.

127513.q: What is meant by the “valley of death” in technology transfer?
a: The funding gap between research and market launch
A valley in Silicon Valley with many bankrupt firms
The time after a patent expires
127513.e: Many inventions fail in the phase when basic research is finished but there is not yet a product ready for the market. Money is often lacking for this risky phase.
127513.m: There is often a funding gap between the lab and the market.

127514.q: Why does a university file a patent for an invention made by its researchers?
a: To protect it and be able to license it to firms
To give it to everyone for free
127514.e: A patent gives the sole right of use for a number of years. The university can license it for fees to firms that turn it into products.
127514.m: Patents make licences to firms possible.

127515.q: What is a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) for, before a university presents an invention to a firm?
a: So that the invention does not become public too early and so no longer count as new
So that the firm does not have to pay tax
So that the invention is automatically patented
So that the university can buy the firm
127515.e: If an invention is made public before the patent is filed, it no longer counts as new. An NDA obliges the people involved in the talks to keep it secret.
127515.m: An NDA protects inventions from being published unintentionally.

127516.q: What do you call a start-up valued at over one billion US dollars that is not listed on the stock exchange?
127516.e: The term “unicorn” was chosen because such firms were very rare at first. It refers to unlisted start-ups valued at one billion dollars or more.
127516.m: A unicorn is a start-up valued at a billion or more.

127517.q: What is the equity called that specialised funds give to young, high-risk firms in exchange for shares?
127517.e: Venture capital funds invest in start-ups with high growth potential and receive stakes in return. Many of these investments fail, but individual successes bring high profits.
127517.m: Venture capital is risk capital in exchange for shares.

127518.q: What do you call a private individual who invests their own money and experience in a start-up early on?
127518.e: Business angels are often experienced entrepreneurs. They invest at an early stage and also support the founders with contacts and advice.
127518.m: A business angel invests money and experience in young firms.

127519.q: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?
a: A first version of a product with only the most necessary features for testing on the market
The product with the lowest price
The final version after all improvements
127519.e: With an MVP, a start-up checks early and cheaply whether customers want the product at all. It is developed further based on the feedback.
127519.m: An MVP tests an idea with as little effort as possible.

127520.q: What does a start-up's “burn rate” describe?
a: How quickly it uses up its capital
How many customers it loses each month
How much profit it makes per product
127520.e: The burn rate shows how much money a start-up that is not yet profitable spends each month. From this you can work out how long the money will last.
127520.m: The burn rate shows how much money is used up each month.

127521.q: What is the very first funding round of a start-up called, often before the product is even finished?
127521.e: In the seed phase, the idea is brought to market readiness with comparatively small amounts. Later come rounds such as Series A, B and C.
127521.m: A start-up begins with seed funding.

127522.q: What typically distinguishes an accelerator from an incubator?
a: A time-limited, intensive programme for start-ups, often in exchange for shares
It only rents out office space without support
It is always a state authority
It only accepts firms with over 100 employees
127522.e: Accelerators support groups of start-ups in a time-limited programme of a few months with coaching and often capital. Incubators usually give longer-term support at an earlier stage.
127522.m: An accelerator speeds up start-ups in a short, intensive programme.

127523.q: What is the minimum share capital you need to found a limited liability company (GmbH) in Switzerland?
127523.e: For a GmbH, the Code of Obligations requires share capital of at least 20,000 francs. For a public limited company (AG), it is at least 100,000 francs.
127523.m: A Swiss GmbH needs at least 20,000 francs of share capital.

127524.q: What is meant by an “exit” for a start-up?
a: The sale of the firm or its stock market listing, when investors turn their shares into money
127524.e: Investors buy into start-ups so that they can make a profit later at the exit. Typical routes are a takeover by another company or a stock market flotation (IPO).
127524.m: At the exit, investors sell their shares at a profit.

127525.q: In which research laboratory was the first working transistor built in 1947?
127525.e: The point-contact transistor was created at the end of 1947 at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the USA. It is regarded as the beginning of semiconductor electronics.
127525.m: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.

127526.q: Which three researchers received the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for developing the transistor?
127526.e: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley were honoured for their research on semiconductors and the discovery of the transistor effect. Bardeen later received a second Nobel Prize in Physics.
127526.m: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley are the fathers of the transistor.

127527.q: Which component did the transistor largely replace in radios and computers?
127527.e: Vacuum tubes were large, fragile and hot, and they used a lot of electricity. Transistors do the same jobs, amplifying and switching, while being much smaller and more economical.
127527.m: The transistor replaced the vacuum tube.

127528.q: Which semiconductor material was the very first transistor of 1947 made of?
127528.e: The first point-contact transistor was built from germanium. Later silicon took over because it withstands heat better and is more common.
127528.m: The first transistor was made of germanium.

127529.q: What is the control terminal of a MOSFET called?
127529.e: In a field-effect transistor (MOSFET), the voltage at the gate controls the current flowing between source and drain. Computer chips contain billions of such MOSFETs.
127529.m: In a MOSFET, the gate controls the current.

127530.q: What did Jack Kilby receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 2000?
a: For his part in inventing the integrated circuit
127530.e: Around 1958 at Texas Instruments, Kilby built one of the first integrated circuits, in which several components are combined on a single piece of semiconductor. Robert Noyce developed a similar solution independently.
127530.m: Jack Kilby is a pioneer of the microchip.

127531.q: What is it called when foreign atoms are deliberately introduced into silicon to create n-type and p-type layers for transistors?
127531.e: Doping with elements such as phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type) creates extra free electrons or holes. Only the combination of such layers makes a transistor possible.
127531.m: Doping turns silicon into a controllable semiconductor.

127532.q: What does the abbreviation LASER stand for?
a: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Spontaneous Energy Release
Linear Amplified Signal of Electronic Radiation
127532.e: A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission. The name describes exactly this physical principle.
127532.m: Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission.

127533.q: Which crystal was the active medium of the first laser?
127533.e: Maiman used a ruby rod that was excited by a flash lamp. The laser produced red light in short pulses.
127533.m: The first laser was a ruby laser.

127534.q: Who described stimulated emission, the basis of the laser, in theory as early as 1917?
127534.e: In his work on the quantum theory of radiation, Einstein introduced stimulated emission. It was only put to technical use in the laser more than 40 years later.
127534.m: Einstein supplied the theory for the laser as early as 1917.

127535.q: Which condition must exist in the active medium for a laser to amplify light?
127535.e: In population inversion, more atoms are in the excited state than in the ground state. Only then does stimulated emission outweigh absorption.
127535.m: Without population inversion there is no laser amplification.

127536.q: What are the two mirrors at the ends of a laser for?
a: They form a resonator in which the light travels back and forth and is amplified
127536.e: In the optical resonator, the light passes through the medium many times and is amplified more and more. One of the mirrors lets some light through, so the laser beam can come out.
127536.m: The resonator made of two mirrors amplifies the laser light.

127537.q: Which property especially distinguishes laser light from the light of a light bulb?
a: It is coherent, so the waves oscillate in step
127537.e: Laser light is coherent, usually of one colour (monochromatic) and tightly focused. Light from a bulb, on the other hand, consists of many wavelengths with random phase.
127537.m: Laser light is coherent and focused.

127538.q: What is the forerunner of the laser called, which works with microwaves instead of visible light?
127538.e: The maser (Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) was developed in the 1950s by Charles Townes and others. Townes received the Nobel Prize for it in 1964.
127538.m: The maser was the microwave forerunner of the laser.

127539.q: Which measuring method uses laser pulses to measure distances and, for example, create 3D maps of terrain?
127539.e: Lidar measures how long laser pulses take to reach an object and come back. This produces precise terrain models, for example for national mapping or for self-driving cars.
127539.m: Lidar measures distances with laser light.

127540.q: Which three researchers received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for the blue light-emitting diode?
127540.e: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura developed efficient blue LEDs in the early 1990s. This made energy-saving white light sources possible.
127540.m: The blue LED earned three Japanese researchers the Nobel Prize.

127541.q: Why does an LED lamp need much less electricity than a light bulb for the same brightness?
a: The light bulb turns most of its energy into heat instead of light
The LED uses sunlight as an extra source
The LED only shines half as brightly
The light bulb needs alternating current, the LED does not
127541.e: In a light bulb, a wire is heated so much that it glows, which mainly produces heat radiation. The LED produces light directly in the semiconductor and loses much less energy as heat.
127541.m: LEDs save electricity because they lose hardly any energy as heat.

127542.q: Why was the blue LED so important for lighting?
a: Only with it could efficient white LED light be produced
Blue light is poisonous to plants
127542.e: Red and green LEDs already existed earlier. Only with blue light could white light be mixed or produced using a phosphor.
127542.m: Without the blue LED there would be no white LED lamps.

127543.q: How is the white light produced in most white LED lamps?
a: A blue LED excites a yellow-glowing phosphor
A red LED is heated strongly
White light is created directly in the silicon
A filament glows inside the LED
127543.e: Part of the blue light is turned into yellow light by the phosphor. Blue and yellow together look white to the eye.
127543.m: White LEDs are blue LEDs with a yellow phosphor.

127544.q: What is the physical effect called by which a light-emitting diode gives off light?
127544.e: In an LED, electrons and holes meet at the p-n junction and release energy as light. This is called electroluminescence, unlike the glowing of a hot wire.

127545.q: What colour were the first LEDs from 1962 that shone in the visible range?
127545.e: In 1962, Nick Holonyak developed a red LED. Bright blue LEDs only followed around 30 years later.
127545.m: The first visible LED shone red.

127546.q: In which storage disc format is a blue-violet laser based on gallium nitride used for reading?
127546.e: Blu-ray players use a laser diode with a wavelength of around 405 nanometres. The shorter wavelength allows smaller data points and therefore more storage space than a DVD.
127546.m: Blu-ray owes its name to the blue laser light.

127547.q: Which three researchers received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the lithium-ion battery?
127547.e: John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino laid the foundations for the rechargeable lithium-ion battery in the 1970s and 1980s.
127547.m: The lithium-ion battery was honoured with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019.

127548.q: What was special about John Goodenough when the Nobel Prize was awarded in 2019?
a: At 97, he was the oldest Nobel laureate so far
He received it for the second time
127548.e: Goodenough was 97 when he was honoured, making him the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize. He died in 2023 at the age of 100.
127548.m: Goodenough is the oldest Nobel laureate.

127549.q: Which company brought the first lithium-ion battery onto the market in 1991?
127549.e: In 1991, Sony sold the first lithium-ion batteries, at first for video cameras. After that they conquered mobile phones, laptops and later electric cars.
127549.m: Sony made the lithium-ion battery ready for the market in 1991.

127550.q: What material is the negative electrode (anode) of most lithium-ion batteries made of?
127550.e: Lithium ions can settle between the layers of graphite during charging. This settling in is called intercalation.
127550.m: The anode of a lithium-ion battery is usually made of graphite.

127551.q: Which metal found in many battery cathodes is criticised because of mining conditions, for example in the Congo?
127551.e: Many lithium-ion batteries contain lithium cobalt oxide, which John Goodenough introduced in 1980. A large share of the cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where work in the mines is often dangerous.
127551.m: Cobalt is a critical raw material for batteries.

127552.q: What happens to the lithium ions when a lithium-ion battery is charged?
a: They move to the negative electrode and settle there
They evaporate out of the battery
They are fused into a block of pure metal
127552.e: During charging, the lithium ions move through the electrolyte to the graphite electrode. During discharging, they return to the positive electrode while the electrons flow through the external circuit.
127552.m: During charging, lithium ions move into the anode.

127553.q: Roughly what nominal voltage does a typical lithium-ion cell with a cobalt cathode have?
127553.e: Lithium-ion cells deliver about three times as much voltage as a nickel-metal hydride cell with 1.2 volts. This contributes to their high energy density.
127553.m: A lithium-ion cell delivers around 3.7 volts.

127554.q: What is the dangerous chain reaction called in which a damaged lithium-ion battery heats up more and more and can catch fire?
127554.e: In thermal runaway, reactions in the battery release heat, which speeds up further reactions. That is why damaged batteries must not be used any longer.
127554.m: Damaged batteries can go into thermal runaway and burn.

127555.q: Where was the scanning tunnelling microscope invented in 1981?
a: At the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon
At Bell Labs in the USA
127555.e: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer developed the device at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. The invention is regarded as an important starting point for nanotechnology.
127555.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope comes from Rüschlikon.

127556.q: Which country did Heinrich Rohrer, one of the inventors of the scanning tunnelling microscope, come from?
127556.e: Heinrich Rohrer was born in Buchs in the canton of St Gallen and studied at ETH Zurich. His colleague Gerd Binnig comes from Germany.
127556.m: Heinrich Rohrer was a Swiss physicist from the canton of St Gallen.

127557.q: In the constant-current mode of a scanning tunnelling microscope, what is recorded to obtain an image of the surface?
a: The up-and-down movement of the tip
127557.e: A control loop keeps the tunnelling current constant by raising or lowering the tip. These height movements produce a height image of the surface, point by point.
127557.m: The up-and-down movement of the tip gives the image of the surface.

127558.q: Why are measurements with a scanning tunnelling microscope for atom-accurate images often carried out in ultra-high vacuum?
a: So that the surface is not contaminated by gas molecules
So that the sample melts faster
So that the tunnelling effect exists at all
So that the tip becomes magnetic
127558.e: In air, foreign molecules settle on the surface within a short time and distort the image. In ultra-high vacuum, a cleaned surface stays clean for a long time; in principle, though, the device also works in air.
127558.m: The vacuum keeps the surface being examined clean.

127559.q: Ideally, what does the very end of a scanning tunnelling microscope's tip look like?
a: It ends in a single atom
It is a ball one millimetre across
It consists of a drop of water
127559.e: Because the tunnelling current depends so strongly on distance, it flows almost only through the frontmost atom. The sharper the tip, the finer the resolution.
127559.m: An ideal measuring tip ends in a single atom.

127560.q: What is used to move the tip of a scanning tunnelling microscope with an accuracy of fractions of a nanometre?
127560.e: Piezo crystals change shape very slightly when an electrical voltage is applied. This allows the tip to be guided extremely finely over the surface.
127560.m: Piezo elements steer the tip with atomic precision.

127561.q: What did IBM researchers achieve for the first time with a scanning tunnelling microscope around 1990?
a: Arranging individual atoms on purpose to spell out letters
Splitting an atom into two parts
Making light faster than in a vacuum
127561.e: Don Eigler and his team pushed 35 xenon atoms on a nickel surface into the letters “IBM”. This showed that matter can be shaped atom by atom.
127561.m: With a scanning tunnelling microscope you can move individual atoms.

127562.q: Which microscope did Gerd Binnig and colleagues develop in 1986 that can also scan non-conducting samples?
127562.e: The atomic force microscope measures the tiny forces between a tip and the surface instead of a current. Today it is also widely used in biology.
127562.m: The atomic force microscope can also scan non-conductors.

127563.q: Which UN specialised agency publishes the Global Innovation Index (GII)?
127563.e: The GII is published by WIPO, based in Geneva, together with partners from science and business. It appears every year.
127563.m: The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO.

127564.q: What rank did Switzerland hold in the Global Innovation Index 2026?
127564.e: Switzerland once again topped the ranking in 2026. It does especially well in research, patents, universities and knowledge output.
127564.m: Switzerland is number one in the Global Innovation Index (as of 2026).

127565.q: Since which year has Switzerland held first place in the Global Innovation Index without a break (as of 2026)?
127565.e: Switzerland has been at the top every year since the 2011 edition. By 2026, that made 16 editions in a row.
127565.m: Switzerland has led the innovation index since 2011.

127566.q: Which country was in 2nd place behind Switzerland in the Global Innovation Index 2026?
127566.e: In 2026, Switzerland was followed by Sweden and the USA. Sweden has been one of the most innovative countries in Europe for years.
127566.m: Sweden came second in the 2026 innovation ranking.

127567.q: Into which two sub-indices is the Global Innovation Index divided?
a: The state and the private sector
127567.e: The input sub-index covers the conditions for innovation, such as institutions and human capital. The output sub-index measures the results, such as knowledge, technology and creative products.
127567.m: The GII compares innovation input with innovation output.

127568.q: What does the Global Innovation Index measure on the output side, among other things?
127568.e: The GII is based on five input pillars and two output pillars. The output side covers knowledge and technology output as well as creative output.
127568.m: On the output side, the GII measures knowledge, technology and creativity.

127569.q: Roughly how many economies are compared in the Global Innovation Index (as of 2026)?
127569.e: The 2026 edition included 139 economies. This means the index covers almost the entire world economy.

127570.q: Why is the Global Innovation Index based on around 80 different indicators instead of just the number of patents?
a: Innovation has many forms and conditions that a single figure cannot capture
127570.e: Besides patents, it includes things like spending on education, research staff, venture capital, high-tech exports and creative goods. This gives a broader picture of the ability to innovate.
127570.m: Innovation is better measured with many indicators than with one figure.

127571.q: What do people do in bionics?
a: Count the stars in the sky
127571.e: In bionics, researchers look closely at how animals and plants solve problems. Then they use these ideas for new technology.

127573.q: Which plant was the model for Velcro?
127573.e: Burdock burrs easily get caught on clothes and fur. Velcro holds in exactly the same way.
127573.m: Velcro was copied from the burdock.

127574.q: Which country did the inventor of Velcro come from?
127574.e: The engineer George de Mestral came from the canton of Vaud. He had his invention protected in the middle of the 20th century.
127574.m: Velcro was invented by a Swiss man.

127575.q: Where did the inventor of Velcro discover lots of burrs?
127575.e: After a walk, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He looked at them closely under the microscope.
127575.m: A walk with the dog gave him the idea for Velcro.

127576.q: What does a burr have on its spines?
127576.e: The spines of the burr end in little hooks. With them, they catch in fur or fabric.
127576.m: A burr holds on with tiny hooks.

127577.q: What does the second side of a Velcro fastener have, which the hooks catch in?
127577.e: One side of the Velcro has hooks, the other lots of soft loops. If you press them together, they catch on each other.
127577.m: Hooks and loops hold Velcro together.

127578.q: What does a bionics expert do first?
127578.e: First you have to understand how an animal or plant does something. Only then can you turn the idea into technology.
127578.m: People who work in bionics observe nature first.

127579.q: What does water do on a lotus leaf?
127579.e: The lotus leaf is water-repellent. Drops of water simply roll over it.
127579.m: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in beads.

127580.q: What do the rolling water drops take with them from the lotus leaf?
127580.e: The rolling drops collect dust and dirt and carry them away. This makes the leaf clean.
127580.m: Water drops wash the lotus leaf clean.

127581.q: What is it called when a leaf keeps itself clean?
127581.e: With the lotus, rain is enough to make the leaf clean again. This is called self-cleaning.
127581.m: The lotus leaf can clean itself.

127582.q: What does the surface of a lotus leaf have when you magnify it a lot?
127582.e: Under the microscope you can see lots of tiny bumps. Drops only touch them in a few places.
127582.m: Tiny bumps make the lotus leaf water-repellent.

127583.q: What else is the lotus leaf covered with?
127583.e: A fine layer of wax repels water. Together with the bumps, this creates the lotus effect.
127583.m: Fine wax helps the lotus leaf repel water.

127584.q: Where does the lotus plant grow?
127584.e: The lotus is a water plant and grows in ponds and lakes. Its large leaves lie on the water or stick up above it.
127584.m: The lotus is a water plant.

127585.q: Which product uses the lotus effect?
127585.e: There are outdoor wall paints with a surface like a lotus leaf. Rain washes the dirt off the wall of the house.
127585.m: Some house paints stay clean thanks to the lotus effect.

127586.q: What colour is the flower of the lotus plant often?
127586.e: The large flowers of the lotus are often pink, sometimes white too. They stick up high above the water.
127586.m: The lotus often has large pink flowers.

127587.q: What shape is a water drop on a lotus leaf?
127587.e: Because the leaf repels the water, the drop pulls together almost into a ball. That way it can roll off easily.
127587.m: On a lotus leaf, drops become almost perfectly round.

127588.q: What does shark skin feel like when you stroke it from the tail to the head?
127588.e: A shark's skin is covered in tiny hard scales. That is why it feels rough when you stroke it the wrong way.
127588.m: Stroked the wrong way, shark skin is rough.

127589.q: What is the surface of shark skin made of?
127589.e: A shark's scales look like little teeth. That is why they are called skin teeth.
127589.m: A shark has tiny teeth on its skin.

127590.q: What do the fine grooves on shark skin help with?
a: Gliding through the water more easily
127590.e: The grooves on the skin teeth guide the water and reduce drag. So the shark swims using less strength.
127590.m: Shark skin helps the shark glide easily through the water.

127591.q: Which sportswear was made with shark skin as a model?
127591.e: Swimsuits with a surface like shark skin were meant to reduce drag in the water. The idea was to swim faster.
127591.m: There were swimsuits modelled on shark skin.

127592.q: What is a ship's paint modelled on shark skin meant to prevent?
a: Mussels and algae growing on it
127592.e: Hardly any algae or mussels settle on the skin of sharks. People want to achieve that for ships too.
127592.m: Shark skin stays free of mussels and algae.

127593.q: Which vehicles are given a film like shark skin to save fuel?
127593.e: A film with tiny grooves reduces air resistance. So aeroplanes need slightly less fuel.
127593.m: Shark-skin film helps aeroplanes save fuel.

127594.q: Which animal group do sharks belong to?
127594.e: Sharks breathe with gills and spend their whole life in water. They are fish.

127595.q: Where can a gecko even walk?
127595.e: Geckos cling so well that they can walk upside down on the ceiling. Even smooth panes of glass are no problem for them.
127595.m: A gecko can walk upside down on the ceiling.

127596.q: What does a gecko have on the underside of its toes?
127596.e: On the toes there are millions of tiny hairs. They get so close to the wall that they stick to it.
127596.m: Fine hairs let the gecko stick to walls.

127597.q: What does a gecko NOT need to stick to a pane of glass?
127597.e: The gecko sticks without any glue. It is only the tiny hairs on its toes that hold it on.
127597.m: A gecko sticks without any glue.

127598.q: Which animal group does the gecko belong to?
127598.e: Geckos are lizards and so they are reptiles. They have scaly skin.

127599.q: What have researchers developed with the gecko as a model?
a: Sticky tape that can be removed again
Glasses that see in the dark
127599.e: Modelled on gecko toes, there are sticky strips without glue. You can remove them and use them again.
127599.m: Gecko tape sticks and can be removed again.

127600.q: When are many geckos out and about?
127600.e: Many types of gecko hunt insects at night. During the day they hide.
127600.m: Many geckos are active at night.

127601.q: How does a gecko get its foot off the wall again?
127601.e: The gecko peels its toes off from the tip like sticky tape. That way it frees its foot very easily.
127601.m: A gecko peels off its toes to let go.

127602.q: What can a gecko shed when in danger?
127602.e: If an enemy grabs the gecko by the tail, it sheds it and escapes. The tail then grows back.
127602.m: A gecko can shed its tail.

127603.q: What does a spider build its web from?
127603.e: The spider makes its threads itself. The material is called spider silk.
127603.m: Spider webs are made of spider silk.

127604.q: Where on the spider are the threads made?
a: On the back part of the body
127604.e: At the end of the back part of its body, the spider has spinnerets. The silk comes out there.
127604.m: The spider spins its threads at the back of its body.

127605.q: A spider's thread is very thin. Does that make it weak?
127605.e: Spider silk is amazingly strong. For its thickness, it can take more than a steel wire of the same thinness.
127605.m: Spider silk is thin but very strong.

127606.q: What can a spider's thread do especially well without breaking?
127606.e: Spider silk is very stretchy. So the web catches a flying insect without tearing.
127606.m: Spider threads are stretchy and do not break easily.

127607.q: What is spider silk made of?
127607.e: Spider silk is made of proteins. Researchers are trying to produce these proteins artificially.
127607.m: Spider silk is made of protein.

127608.q: What would people like to use artificial spider silk for, for example?
127608.e: Spider silk is strong and the body accepts it well. So it could be used in medicine, for example for stitches.
127608.m: Artificial spider silk could help in medicine.

127609.q: Why doesn't a spider get stuck in its own web?
a: It walks on threads that are not sticky
It washes the web with water
127609.e: Not all the threads in the web are sticky. The spider walks mainly on the dry threads.
127609.m: The spider knows the dry threads in its web.

127610.q: What does a spider catch with its web?
127610.e: Flies, mosquitoes and other insects get caught in the web. The spider then eats them.
127610.m: Spiders catch insects in their webs.

127611.e: Many types of termite build large mounds. A whole colony lives inside.

127612.q: What do termites build their mounds from?
127612.e: Termites mix soil with their saliva. When the mixture dries, it becomes rock hard.
127612.m: Termite mounds are built from soil and saliva.

127613.q: What provides fresh air in a termite mound?
127613.e: Air flows through the mound through many tunnels and shafts. This keeps it pleasant inside.
127613.m: Tunnels and channels air the termite mound.

127614.q: On which continent is there a well-known office building that is aired like a termite mound?
127614.e: In Zimbabwe, a large building was built that airs itself on the model of termite mounds. That is why it needs much less energy for ventilation and cooling.
127614.m: A building in Africa airs itself like a termite mound.

127615.q: What does a building designed like a termite mound save?
127615.e: The air is cooled without big machines. That is why the building needs much less electricity.

127616.e: Termites like warmth. Most kinds live in the tropics and other warm areas.
127616.m: Termites live mainly in warm countries.

127617.q: How high can termite mounds get?
127617.e: Some termite mounds are taller than an adult. They can be several metres high.
127617.m: Termite mounds can be several metres high.

127618.e: Many termites eat wood and other plant parts. That is why they can also damage wooden houses.

127619.e: The boxfish has an angular body. It looks like a little box.
127619.m: The boxfish is square like a box.

127620.q: What surrounds the body of the boxfish?
127620.e: The boxfish lives inside a shell of bony plates. Only its fins, eyes and mouth stick out.
127620.m: The boxfish wears a hard shell.

127621.q: What was built with the boxfish as a model?
127621.e: A car maker built a test car in the shape of the boxfish. It was meant to have little air resistance.
127621.m: A car was modelled on the boxfish.

127622.q: What does the boxfish mainly swim with?
a: Its whole body like a snake
A jet of water like a squid
127622.e: The hard shell can hardly bend. That is why the boxfish moves mainly with its small fins.
127622.m: The boxfish swims with its fins.

a: In the sea near coral reefs
127623.e: Boxfish live in warm seas. They are often found near coral reefs.
127623.m: The boxfish lives in the sea near corals.

127624.q: What does the young yellow boxfish look like?
127624.e: The young yellow boxfish is bright yellow and has black spots. The colour warns enemies.
127624.m: The young yellow boxfish is yellow with black spots.

127625.q: What can the boxfish release when in danger?
127625.e: The boxfish can release poison through its skin. This protects it from enemies.
127625.m: The boxfish protects itself with poison.

127626.q: What did engineers learn from the boxfish's shell?
a: How to build light but strong
How to build as heavy as possible
How to build only with glass
How to build only round parts
127626.e: The boxfish's shell is light and yet very strong. This is also useful for cars and machines.
127626.m: The boxfish shows how to build light and strong.

127627.q: Which vehicle was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak?
127627.e: Engineers in Japan shaped the front of a high-speed train like a kingfisher's beak. The kingfisher was a good model for this.
127627.m: A Japanese high-speed train has a nose like a kingfisher.

127628.q: What problem did the high-speed train in Japan used to have when leaving a tunnel?
127628.e: The train pushed the air in the tunnel along in front of it. When it came out, there was a loud bang.
127628.m: The new train nose helped against the bang at the tunnel.

127629.q: How does the kingfisher dive into the water?
127629.e: The kingfisher's beak is shaped so that it slides into the water with almost no splash. That is why it was a good model.
127629.m: The kingfisher dives in with almost no splash.

127630.q: What does the kingfisher mainly eat?
127630.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch over the water. When it sees a small fish, it plunges in.

127631.q: What colour is the kingfisher's back?
127631.e: The kingfisher has a bright blue back and an orange breast. It is one of the most colourful birds in Switzerland.
127631.m: The kingfisher has a bright blue back.

127632.q: Where can you watch kingfishers in Switzerland?
127632.e: The kingfisher needs clear water with small fish. That is why it lives by water.
127632.m: You find the kingfisher by water.

127633.q: What did the high-speed train with the kingfisher nose need less of than before?
127633.e: With the new nose, the train has to push away less air. That is why it uses less electricity.
127633.m: The kingfisher nose saves the train electricity.

127634.q: Where does the kingfisher make its nest?
a: In a tunnel in an earth bank
127634.e: The kingfisher digs a tunnel into a steep earth bank by the water. The nest is at the end of the tunnel.
127634.m: The kingfisher nests in a tunnel in the riverbank.

127635.q: What does the humpback whale have on the front edge of its flippers?
127635.e: The front edge of the flipper is not smooth but has lots of bumps. It looks like a row of lumps.
127635.m: The humpback whale's flipper has bumps.

127636.q: What do the bumps on its flippers help the humpback whale to do?
127636.e: The bumps guide the water well around the flipper. So the big whale can swim in surprisingly tight turns.
127636.m: Thanks to the bumps, the humpback whale is very agile.

127637.q: Which machines were given blades with bumps modelled on the humpback whale?
127637.e: Rotor blades with bumps like the humpback whale's are meant to use the wind better. Fans have also been built this way.
127637.m: Some wind turbines have bumps like the humpback whale.

127638.q: What is special about the humpback whale's flippers?
127638.e: The humpback whale has the longest flippers of all whales. They are about a third as long as its body.
127638.m: The humpback whale has very long flippers.

127639.q: Which animal group does the humpback whale belong to?
127639.e: Whales breathe with lungs and feed their young with milk. That is why they are mammals, even though they live in the sea.
127639.m: The humpback whale is a mammal.

127640.q: What are humpback whales famous for?
127640.e: Male humpback whales sing long songs made of many sounds. They can be heard far away underwater.

127641.q: What does the humpback whale eat?
127641.e: The humpback whale has no teeth, but baleen plates. With them, it sieves krill and small fish out of the water.
127641.m: The humpback whale eats krill and small fish.

127642.q: How does the humpback whale drive fish together into a shoal?
a: With a net of air bubbles
127642.e: The humpback whale swims in a circle and blows out air bubbles. The fish stay trapped in this bubble net.
127642.m: Humpback whales hunt with a net of air bubbles.

127643.q: What does a streamlined shape look like?
